quote: Is there a charge for this?
stewart_read: This is a cost/trust objection right at the door; rep explains the business model reasonably but never flips it toward her actual bill pain.
alternative_hypothesis: Reactive read: rep answered literally instead of using the moment to anchor on her utility bill as the real cost. Strategic read not supported — no later bill-flip occurs either.
coaching_implication: Suggested rephrase: 'No upfront charge — the real cost is what ComEd is already charging you every month.' Ties cost fear to bill pain immediately.

stewart_read: A financial-hardship disclosure is a trust gift; rep's response ('Gotcha. Yeah. We we definitely love to help...') is generic and moves straight back to pitch.
coaching_implication: Should acknowledge specifically and check in before continuing — e.g. ask what she means by that in relation to affording changes, not just restate the value prop.

quote: Well, I live on Social Security.
stewart_read: Second vulnerability disclosure, directly relevant to the income-tax qualifier being asked about, and rep pivots straight to credit score without addressing the income implication.
alternative_hypothesis: Reactive read is strongest: the rep needed this info to properly assess the tax-credit qualifier (SSI often means no income tax liability) but treated it as noise rather than a disqualifying signal to explore.
coaching_implication: Rep should have asked whether she pays federal income tax at all, since the tax credit qualifier explicitly requires income tax liability — this is a hard-gate question being glossed over.

quote: you're just gonna be paying income tax and have a credit score above six fifty.
stewart_read: Rep bundles two separate hard qualifiers (income tax liability + 650 credit) into one run-on statement, and never separately confirms either — customer answers vaguely and rep accepts it as confirmed ('you should be good to go').
coaching_implication: Split the qualifier into two explicit yes/no questions; don't mark 'good to go' when the customer never actually confirmed either condition.

quote: Oh, I I I don't know. I didn't really know. Sorry.
stewart_read: Customer explicitly doesn't know her credit score, which should trigger a clear script branch, but instead the rep improvises a manager-check hold.
alternative_hypothesis: Strategic read: checking with a manager could be legitimate escalation for an edge case. But the rep frames it uncertainly himself ('let's see... let me check with him'), suggesting he doesn't know the correct procedure rather than deliberately invoking one.
coaching_implication: This is exactly the kind of edge case (unknown credit + SSI income) that needs a defined script branch — flag for Kenny calibration on qualifiers.credit_qualifier drift.

quote: I'll check with my manager to see what he thinks
stewart_read: Call ends on a five-minute callback promise with no locked appointment time, no button-up handshake, and the qualifying gate still open.
coaching_implication: Even a short callback should get a time-specific commitment and a verbal handshake; here it's just 'about five minutes' with no confirmation the customer will actually be reached or the deal is viable.

quote: I was watching a YouTube video when a commercial came on for this.
stewart_read: Weak, low-depth interest reason given; rep accepts it with a one-line acknowledgment and moves straight to pulling up the roof rather than probing for real motivation (bill pain, environment, etc).
coaching_implication: This reason was never expanded or used later to anchor the appointment — a deeper follow-up question here could have surfaced actual bill pain motivation.
